63.t: Cancelling a Southern tour when promoters wanted Lips Page seated 15 feet away
63.s: Booking agents proposed that Page sit fifteen feet from the band; Shaw cancelled the tour, noting Zutty Singleton had been in his first band.
63.ch: Billie Holiday, band members and singers
63.q: Nobody knows that. He was in the band. We played in Atlantic City. Zutty was a nice little drummer for that band. Perfect. He played quietly. He used to turn his head like this. I loved him. A nice guy. Anyway, there was always a colored guy somewhere in there. Couldn’t have too many. Even Benny…

63.t: Billie's Southern tour and the heckler who ended it
63.s: Shaw talks Billie into singing in front of a white band in the South; a redneck heckler's slur led to a near riot and her removal from the tour.
63.ch: Billie Holiday, band members and singers
63.q: said, “Come on. You’re joining the band.” She said, “What are you talking about?” This is like three in the morning. We finished a gig in Boston, drove down to New York. At that hour you could make it in about three hours. Got to Harlem about 3:30 maybe and woke her up. She came out, rubbing her…

63.t: The Hotel Lincoln freight elevator and Billie leaving the band
63.s: The hotel manager asked that Billie use the freight elevator; Shaw left the decision to her, she gave notice to go solo, and Down Beat blamed Shaw. He adds that Vegas rooms barred his black sidemen in the 1950s.
63.ch: Billie Holiday, band members and singers
63.q: It was too difficult. It was just going to be too tough. Same as Roy [Eldridge]. I’ll tell you a story about Roy, how he got out, how he left the band. He’s told the story, but he’s not told it the way it was. I can understand. He’s a little embarrassed by it. He was then. Anyway, I hired Helen.…

63.t: Roy Eldridge in the band: salary, segregation and the knife
63.s: Eldridge was paid top money but was barred from a San Francisco auditorium as a gate-crasher, was given notice, and confronted Shaw with a knife.
63.ch: Billie Holiday, band members and singers
63.q: Later on, when Roy was in the band, I paid Roy the highest price going at that time. I think it was 500 bucks a week. Today that would be roughly a couple of thousand, maybe three thousand. It was a good salary. The rest of the band, the most a man, any other man got was two or three hundred.…

232.t: Dewey Goosby calls him off the bandstand
232.s: Goosby calls pretending to be Fields' wife, complaining that Black patrons are not being admitted to the white dance.
232.ch: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
232.q: So I guess maybe we were playing for about a half hour or more and I got a call-- I wouldn't like to be disturbed on the bandstand and I told them if anybody called that I'm just busy, unless it's very important, don't call me off the bandstand, and that's the order that I had given.

232.t: The union agent and the policeman who called Iller a creole
232.s: Parker Berry's worry about a mixed band is realised when the union agent and officer question Iller, and Fields settles it by saying he looks white but is creole.
232.ch: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
232.q: Parker, when we were fixing to go, he said I don't know if you can; I said what. So he said something about Nat King and some concert and they stopped him because he had a mixed band or something, and he said you didn't say anything about that and I said no, oh Parker.

232.t: Getting Goosby's party into McElroy's ballroom
232.s: Fields advises Goosby on how to demand admission, and Pops McElroy admits his party free.
232.ch: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
232.q: Well, this stuff that we can't go and I know you can tell them to let us in, we have our money and we got to break down this

232.t: The Tougaloo dentist and Sammy Edwards' toothache
232.s: A white dentist pulls drummer Sammy Edwards' tooth on his porch so no white patient will see a Black man in his chair.
232.q: And another thing, he would watch everything, and in the south--he would say a lot of things, but this wasn't anything malicious, but he had--I just wish I had the picture because it's just so comical to think how this race issue was so simple. I believe it was Tougaloo, Mississippi that we were…

80.t: Fats refuses the South, then plays Fort Lauderdale under Florida's segregation law
80.s: Fats had avoided the South; at the Fort Lauderdale date a white friend could not sit with them under state law and the white manager could not take tickets inside, so counted the crowd from the bus.
80.ch: Hopkins, the South and Stuff Smith
80.q: They did not mix it. And that's another thing, we played Florida with Fats, first time Fats went to Florida they offered him, oh, man, they offered him a mint to come. For he wouldn't take it. Fats had never been south in his life, and all he heard was stories that he didn't want any parts of it.…

80.t: Refused service at a Michigan border diner
80.s: Coming out of Canada, a waitress in the North told his band 'We don't serve your kind', which shocked him more than the South had.
80.ch: Hopkins, the South and Stuff Smith
80.q: Yeah, that's what I mean. So now we came back to Ohio, I mean Illinois, Michigan. We played Canada now. We come out of Canada, going into Detroit, we stopped at the border, and we get some -- we saw a joint -- hot dogs, and crap, so we got out and ordered for the -- I did, several of us, and…

80.t: The ice cream cone, and being treated warmly in Southern white restaurants
80.s: He recalls his father steering him past a whites-only ice cream shop; on southern tours of the thirties he sometimes found white restaurants unexpectedly friendly.
80.ch: Hopkins, the South and Stuff Smith
80.q: Uh, I'm trying to think. Yeah, I have -- I'm trying to pin it down, because you would run into -- I'm glad you asked me that, because being born in the South I knew what to expect, and I knew what one could do, should do, or shouldn't do.

121.t: Family and whites; touring the South in the civil rights era
121.s: His family had no trouble with whites; on tour he was treated well, with stories of Mississippi and a dance hall where bands played each song twice.
121.ch: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
121.q: You know, okay, first of all, I can say this. You see, my family being the type of people that they were, we never did have no white problem. We never had no white. You know what, I think it's because I think being from a decent family, I think we were kind of looked on as just poor, decent people.…

121.t: Staying on the bandstand at white dances, and playing Dixie
121.s: Rules of not mingling at white dances, how he felt, and insisting his band play Dixie.
121.ch: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
121.q: People could come ask us things, but you just didn't go out there and touch, or talk, or mingle, or nothing. And like I said, when you come off the bandstand, you walk side the bandstand. You don't go out, you walk side the bandstand, round down to the bathroom.

153.t: Segregation on the Big Show tour and Mississippi hospitality
153.s: The 1951 package tour in the segregated South, Bellson passing as Haitian, and townspeople hosting the band in Mississippi.
153.q: Well yes, we did have. In 1951 they had the Big Show of 1951, which consisted of Nat King Cole, Sarah Vaughan and Duke Ellington’s band. They were the three big stars. Now besides that they had Peg Leg Bates, Timmy Rodgers, Stump and Stumpy, Patterson and Jackson, all these wonderful acts — tap…

153.t: The segregated Big Show of 1951 tour as a Haitian drummer
153.s: On the tour with Nat Cole and Sarah Vaughan he faced Jim Crow, Duke had him pass as Haitian, and some Southerners hosted them kindly.
153.ch: Small bands, Harry James and joining Duke Ellington
153.q: It was beautiful. Every guy in that band was beautiful. It’s a family. It was a family band. We shared everything. Even on that tour. You were asking about that tour, Big Show of 1951? The three main characters were Duke Ellington’s band, Sarah Vaughan, and Nat “King” Cole. That was really…

351.t: Austin ballroom applause and a dangerous Florida hall
351.s: Hungry stop on a broken-down bus, a standing ovation in Austin, and a West Palm Beach hall with the stand raised high.
351.q: waiting and now it’s like 5 or 6:00 and the guys were getting hungry. So the manager was the white guy, Frenchie — excuse me, the ginger ale, it’s human, it’s real — so we said you know we just passed a diner about a hundred feet back there. So the guy that sold the programs, Frenchie and myself,…

351.t: Threats from Texas men and first encounters with Jim Crow
351.s: A confrontation outside a Texas club, then restaurants and water fountains in the South.
351.q: I said, “I’m getting paid to work with him, you’re a bigger jerk than I am, aren’t you?” And just as I said that, Cozy was coming out to call me or something, and he heard me say that. He says, “Marty, telephone.” So he came to grab me and he pulled me in. He says, “are you crazy?” I said, “what?”…

164.t: Dorsey standing up for Charlie Shavers in Virginia
164.s: Dorsey walked the band out of a restaurant that would not serve Shavers.
164.q: Well Dorsey was very good at that. That’s one thing — Tommy would not stand for any hassles of Charlie. He was the only guy in the band that had a tan and when you play in Virginia and all that routine. There was one night, I wasn’t there at the time, because Louie and I were driving in our…

164.t: Being Charlie Shavers' bodyguard and rejecting racial divisions
164.s: He guarded Charlie Shavers on a Southern tour with Dorsey and says the color line has no place in music.
164.q: along in the business to avoid any of the pitfalls you might have run into, you should do it. You owe that to this business. Don’t get into racial scenes. I used to be Charlie Shaver’s bodyguard when we did a tour of the south. I mean I would go to the men’s room with him.

368.t: Muncie, Indiana: the club owner wants the black players in the cellar
368.s: He refused to separate his band, and they stayed together at the band table.
368.ch: The Blakey quartet on the road
368.q: That was with a group. Kenny Drew, Art Blakey, and Eugene Wright were with me. Three black guys and myself, I was white. And we, we played at this club, we hadn’t played there before, and when we got there we set up the band stand, set up the bass and drums and everything in the afternoon and spoke…

368.t: Motel eviction at 3 a.m. and walking out of the Muncie job
368.s: The motel ordered the black players out, so the whole group packed up and left for Chicago.
368.ch: The Blakey quartet on the road
368.q: Yeah. But, you know, they were sensible enough to know this arrangement would work and we could get through the job. We didn’t want to blow the job, totally. None of us wanted to. And finally, we had a fantastic night. I mean, a successful night. The audience loved the group and we left, got in our…

101.t: Town Hall concert and the Washington drugstore incident
101.s: The 1947 Town Hall album, Neal Hefti and Severinsen in the band, and the band's revenge when a hotel drugstore would not serve Black musicians.
101.q: We did – the only that I know of that the band ever did, we did at Town Hall. I think that was in ’47. We did Charleston Alley and Gal from Joe’s and tunes of that sort. I don’t recall any other particular things that we did. We were on the road for a bunch of the time. Neal Hefti wrote for the…

101.s: The first session partly inaudible; Barnet dressed Terry and Nottingham in gray, provoking audience protest in Washington.

165.t: Insisting on a non-segregation clause for Austin, Texas
165.s: The trio demanded a non-segregated clause, ignored Basie's warning, and had a great time in Austin.
165.ch: Vocalese and Lambert, Hendricks and Ross
165.q: I think that since I never had anything other than a spiritual approach to those things, the impact was minimal on me. I think most artists share this with each other. That’s why I think I became an artist, because they don’t look at things like race. They look at what you do, and if they like it,…

165.t: Starving after Sing a Song of Basie and his father's teaching on race
165.s: The trio was broke even with a number 13 album; Hendricks recalls his father's lesson that every person is your sibling.
165.ch: Vocalese and Lambert, Hendricks and Ross
165.q: Sing a Song of Basie. The album was number 13 in Down Beat. Dave and I were starving, literally starving. We were starving. Dave had an account at Joe’s Dinette. We went over there every night for dinner. Joe somehow knew we were going to be something one day, and he put it on this tab. The tab was…

226.t: Refused rooms at a Salt Lake City hotel
226.s: A desk clerk refused Denzil Best and Al McKibbon; the band stayed in a Pullman porters' rooming house.
226.ch: From bassist to George Shearing's road manager
226.q: I had a lot of little incidents like that that happened. We got to Salt Lake City. Everything was all set. We were doing a big concert there, the first time in Salt Lake City. The first that happened, we drive up to the hotel. We’ve got Denzil Best, Al McKibbon, Chuck Wayne, George Shearing, and…

226.t: Road manager stories: the Omaha piano and the St. Louis disc jockey
226.s: Club owners and a disc jockey did not know Levy was black; he made an Omaha owner move the piano and refused a DJ's request that Shearing sit in a segregated audience.
226.ch: From bassist to George Shearing's road manager
226.q: bass and help them do this, that I needed to be – he needed to get somebody else to play bass and for me to become the road manager. He tried to get a road manager while I was the bass player. Cliff Arenson was one of them. He was an agent – Cliff Arenson was an agent for Joe Glaser that had helped…

376.t: Segregated hotels, Bill Clark's name and Joe Wilder in the pool
376.s: He recalls separate hotels in Washington and Baltimore, the Bill Clark correction and Joe Wilder's swim.
376.q: Yeah, but [different?] in some, some places. Even in Washington, when I joined the George Shearing Quartet, it was… when was it? ’52, ’53, maybe… 53? There was a club, a restaurant club where we played. Olivia, Olivia’s Lounge Hotel Restaurant. I think Club and Lounge on the first floor. And there…

376.t: Traveling the South and the Ray Charles jukebox
376.s: Only two white guys on the bus; at stops everyone raced to the jukebox for Ray Charles.
376.q: And each time we stopped, everybody was fighting to get to the juke box, put a quarter or whatever it was, a quarter, to hear that Ray Charles song. [laughs] Well, that’s worthwhile talking about, I think.

406.t: A college dance, a fraternity party and Max reciting the Gettysburg Address
406.s: After the dance Barefield urged leaving the fraternity house before the troopers arrived. At a Howard Johnson's that would not serve them, Max stood on a stool reciting the Gettysburg Address.
406.q: So we finally went on to this college to play this -- play this concert or dance. I think It was a dance. And there was a lot of Northern kids at this college from New York and everything. So the thing went over good. So they invited us to the frat house after we got through.

406.t: Max Kaminsky's mixed band cannot find a motel in Virginia
406.s: Traveling to Virginia with a band of three black and three white players, they were turned away at motels. Barefield found a rooming house near the tracks and fried chicken.
406.q: You know, we had a band one time through the -- and I think -- I don't know what years it was, but it was in the '40s or '50s or something like that, and it was Max Kaminsky's band, Dixieland band. And they had Dick Carey on piano.

1.t: Waiting by the garbage cans to see the Senator
1.s: Because they were Black, Danny, Lu and Paul had to enter the Senator's hotel through the basement and waited hours, and Lu refused to return.
1.ch: Cab Calloway's band, Hadacol and closing reflections
1.q: Me, you and Paul. Because they wanted him to bring me, because he was supposed to bring me a watch. So we go to the hotel, and we couldn't go through the front door. So we had to go around. So we're finally in the basement. I'm all sharp, you know, and I was young...

1.t: Dinner at the Roosevelt and a horse of another color
1.s: When the Senator invited them to the Roosevelt, Danny said they were Colored, and the Senator, thinking Lu was white, changed his plan.
1.ch: Cab Calloway's band, Hadacol and closing reflections
1.q: Now, what happened, Paul said, "Man, that's wonderful, because Senator Lebeau has got gangs of station wagons. We were using Paul's little truck. That's before we got the bus. He had a little small station wagon. But it was hard carrying seven musicians and her. So we all piled up in this little...

229.t: The Santa Barbara hotel incident with Lionel's band
229.s: On Hampton's first tour in 1935 the band was put out of a Santa Barbara hotel after the owner found they were Black.
229.ch: The Legends of Jazz and life on the road
229.q: We got to Santa Barbara early, we had to play two nights there, so we got there in time to go to the jobs. So we didn't look for any place to stay until after we got to work. So we went to work that first night, Gladys was the boss, she was the head of the band, unofficially, and she goes to the…

229.t: The Georgia Minstrels tour and prejudice North and South
229.s: He describes the 1932-33 Georgia Minstrels season booked by Fanchon Marco and says audiences in the South were kinder than in the North.
229.ch: The Legends of Jazz and life on the road
229.q: of that. In my career I missed one season tour I made with the Georgia Minstrels, and they were booked by Fanchon Marco; they had more people working for them than any agency in the country at that time.

113.t: Stanley Dance's South America story and talk of Jim Crow laws
113.s: Stanley recalls being refused boarding in Brazil with Ellington's band because he was white; McShann and Stanley agree such laws were a hangover from slavery.

113.t: Segregation on the road and the white trumpeter at the filling station
113.s: Prompted by Earl Warren's stories, he tells how a white trumpet player in his band was sent to the colored restroom at a southern gas station.
113.q: And then a lot of times, he'd probably have to go get food for them. You know? And it's funny, but it's true. I had a white fella that was playing with me. We were down South one time. And I think it was going through either Georgia or Alabama and we stopped to get gas and that's when they had…

566.t: Racism: Norman Granz insisting on hotels and train service
566.s: Humes says she has not had trouble with racism and wonders why. Norman Granz made hotels that excluded Black guests accept the JATP company and got the best train accommodations, and she saw no friction among performers.
566.q: Maybe, it's something because I don't have problems like that. I remember, now the fellow that really did a whole lot was Norman Granz. Norman used to take us places and go in hotels where they didn't have colored. Norman said, they're going to stay here, and we stayed, and everybody was so sweet.…

566.t: One-nighters in the South, Earle Warren on the train and Basie's bridges
566.s: One-nighters through the South were rough. Light-skinned Earle Warren was told to leave the white coach, and later got food for the band in segregated towns. Basie would get off the bus to walk across rickety bridges.
566.q: in the coach with us and the conductor came and he said, "look here you, you got to get out of here". Earle said, "I don't know why". And he said, "we don't have no mixed". Earle said, "well I'm not white". He said, "you ain't fooling us. You go on up there in the next car". And then when Earle got…

148.t: Hostile Southern audiences and the absence of black players on tour
148.s: Audiences in the South and Southwest were hostile, and black stars joined only in the north; Trummy Young stayed longest.
148.ch: The Raeburn band: people and touring
148.q: Of course, I also recall how hostile audiences were in certain parts of the country, just by nature of the fact that we came from New York, we came down to play for them. They would sit there, you know, impress me, show me something. They never applauded, just sat there.

148.t: Bothwell's missed Basie job and lost library
148.s: Schremp says Bothwell was asked to join Basie but could not tour the South as a white lead alto; his library was lost.
148.ch: The Raeburn band: people and touring
148.q: Not Duke's band, but the Basie band, but he couldn't do it for the reverse reason that they couldn't take that black band through the South with a white lead alto player. They might have a white fourth trumpet player and get by with it, but they couldn't have a white lead alto player, so he lost…

169.t: Being a Black man in Barnet's band: the Worcester hotel
169.s: Barnet does not tolerate prejudice, but the road manager fails to book rooms for McGhee and Holland in Worcester, and Barnet fires him.
169.ch: Hampton, Andy Kirk and Charlie Barnet
169.q: No, wasn't no problems with the people in the band. Charlie wouldn't go for that shit. If you was prejudiced, you didn't have no business being there, and he let you know that right away.

169.t: Barnet band details: no Southern tours, 'Strollin'' and the rhythm section
169.s: The band never went below the Mason-Dixon Line; McGhee wrote 'Strollin'' and other pieces; he lists the rhythm section and Barnet's temper.
169.ch: Hampton, Andy Kirk and Charlie Barnet
169.q: : Yeah, we played the Apollo several times. In fact, we played everywhere, except anywhere below the Mason-Dixon Line. We'd never go down there.

19.t: Washington dance, segregation in the South, and drummer Charlie Buck quits
19.s: With a white drummer unable to go South, Malachi brings in Charlie Buck, who flees back to Washington after meeting Jim Crow at Rocky Mount.
19.q: Anyway, we made this dance that night, and this was our first dance in Wilmington, Delaware. The next one was in Washington, D.C., and I think it was at Turner's Arena up at Fourteenth and W Streets. We played this dance, and now everybody's wondering what's going to happen, because at that…

19.t: Improvised drummers across the South and the white drummer sent home
19.s: From Columbia, South Carolina, to Tampa they use whatever drummer they can find, while the distressed white New Yorker is sent back.
19.q: bandstand with this great, big bass drum, which had a picture of a moon and a river on it... Heh-heh... He just had an odd-looking set of drums with him. If anything, it was this big bass drum... So everybody's saying, "Oh my God, what's going to happen?" But at least he made a picture of we're…

402.t: Playing in Alabama, Selma and visiting Montgomery
402.s: Sal describes working the Dixie Club near an air base, and a trip to Montgomery.
402.q: Well, I didn't travel much. I just played around Louisiana here. A few times, I'd sit like Corksdale. And Alabama, you played? Alabama, I played in Tuscaloosa, Basma, what the hell the name of that plays? Well, integration thing, huh? Selma. Selma. Oh man, I played that. The man said, honey, well,…

251.t: Fear of restaurants and being unwanted
251.s: Albert still feels uneasy in restaurants; Roland Kirk anecdote.
251.q: To eat dinner? Yeah. Well, I'll tell you what, Dick. I still am reluctant to go to cafeterias or cafes. I don't do too much of it now. I never did. I like to eat at home, but my wife and my daughter, every now and then they'll say, Daddy, let's go get something to eat at the Luby's or one of the…

83.t: Sharing a train car with Tommy Ridgley
83.s: Matassa and Ridgley rode the same car to New York despite segregation, with the train splitting in Florida and the Pullman porter staying silent.
83.q: Oh, we joked about that, you know, because it wasn't legal in those days, you know. Black Iron One, and I think I was in the upper company.

270.t: Traveling now and playing up north
270.s: Travels on concert tours and with the Chocolate Music Bars, and racial attitudes up north.
270.q: Yeah, we have some. We were, well, we were, well, we were, well, we were, You heard what I said about my travel thing I did. Before, 24, I went to Chicago, I was waiting for this track for the steamboat line, and then there's a preservation hall. I know what they expected, and how they carry them,…

632.t: Lizzie Miles and racial attitudes in 1940s New Orleans
632.s: They discuss Lizzie Miles with an all-white band, how black performers dealt with segregation, and her anger over the library not admitting her.
632.q: Yeah. I heard Lizzie, oh, a number of times. I don't remember a great deal about her. I kind of liked her. I kind of liked her sometimes. Other times, she was a little bit too much, for my taste, more of a showwoman than a blues singer. And what I was interested in at the time, particularly, was…

194.t: Racial barriers and rough Chalmette audiences
194.s: He says he never had racial trouble with mixed groups until the 1970s in Chalmette.
194.q: I never was bothered with it myself. I mean I've been playing with mixed groups and mixed houses all my life. I was raised up with white people to tell you the truth of them.

58.s: They recall being treated well in Des Moines and Canada.
58.q: Big Royal American show, we'd go there every year.

905.t: Racial mixing in the music, Punch Miller and Page Hotel
905.s: Allen and Mrs. Phillips talk about mixed-race groups and segregation; Punch Miller's whereabouts and name.
905.q: I almost got arrested with another night. They just don't like it. And it ain't no use of trying to put it over. They don't like it. And it's been going on before you, you, me or him was born. That mix. And they ain't gonna never break it up. Oh, no. Well, I mean, you just gotta sit in. They ain't…

676.t: Segregation in Denver and Marie Bryant's St. Louis theater story
676.s: Quinichette's family in the Denver balcony episode, and Marie Bryant passing in a St. Louis theater.
676.q: Yes, or worse. When we were in Denver, Shorty Sherock and this mixed band, we became very friendly with Paul Quinichette and his wife, and his mother who a was darling and attractive woman who was a businesswoman. I think she did real estate or something like that. And so one night we were going to…

603.q: I think so. Yeah. The difference didn’t seem so physical as it was metaphysical. Very strange. I still have a bad taste in my mouth from it. We also went to see — we were working a club in Shreveport, Louisiana and it was called the Great American City the sign said as we pulled in. And I saw in…

203.t: Billie Holiday and racism on the road with Shaw
203.s: Incidents with Billie Holiday and Zutty Singleton in West Virginia, New England, and the Lincoln Hotel kitchen door.
203.ch: Biagini, Duke and the Shaw band

435.t: Dave Brubeck's 1976 South African tour and its conditions
435.s: The New Brubeck Quartet toured on conditions of a black support act, a black bassist (Vic Ntoni) and unsegregated audiences; Cathy acted as liaison.

579.t: Dignity of veteran Black musicians and racism
579.s: Rowe notes their lack of bitterness; Gourse says they used humor, avoided the South and still carry prejudice from the past.
579.q: Well I think it’s just part of not letting life in general, the negative take over. Sometimes to keep themselves sane they made up funny stories that happened to them. Sometimes they would tell stories that were very, very touching and from just one incident you get the feeling of the whole mess.…

328.t: Segregation on tour and music above racism
328.s: Few problems in the integrated band except a southern tour; with Buddy Johnson they could not eat or stay in hotels; musicians kept playing jazz even under the Nazis.
328.ch: Road to New York and Maynard Ferguson
328.q: I think the only time that we had any problems like that was when we took a whole tour. It was Sonny Rollins and his quartet, or no it was the trio, and it was Dave Brubeck with his group, Maynard Ferguson’s band. And then there was another, might have been The Four Freshmen or somebody like that.…

330.t: Al Hibbler, Monty Alexander and being refused service in Miami
330.s: With Hibbler in Miami in 1965, he met Monty Alexander and a waitress refused to serve 'the colored'.
330.q: good experience. But then when that ran dry I went to work with Al Hibbler. And Al Hibbler and I were in Miami, Florida, playing in a hotel/bar type place that had a restaurant. This was in 1965. And as a matter of fact this was the same year I met Monty Alexander. Monty came in that same night and…

209.t: First encounter with racial prejudice in Spokane
209.s: The band's one black tenor player was barred from the Spokane ballroom park, which shocked Hardaway. He recalls the player as Walter Benton, and Hardaway took over the jazz tenor chair.
209.ch: First road band and learning jazz
209.q: The family name was Cascales actually. And that was the first time I was ever exposed to any sort of racial prejudice as well was at that time.

411.t: Segregation on tour and the 1954 Kenton festival bus
411.s: Segregated southern audiences, Art Tatum's trio unable to leave the bus on the Kenton tour, and wartime Marine experiences of racism.
411.ch: Road life, race and Woody Herman/Tommy Dorsey
411.q: Oh yeah. But the problem was that when you got down south they couldn’t mingle. You know they’d have, of course then everybody was colored.

421.t: Segregation in Kansas City and Alabama
421.s: The club was not segregated but Kansas City was; he recalls being thrown out of an Earl Hines show in Alabama in 1933-34.
421.q: No, no the place was not segregated at all. But the feeling in Kansas City was. Blacks were blacks and whites were whites. That’s the way it was.

670.s: She describes roped-off dance halls with Buddy Johnson and a 1960 night in Georgia when she stayed outside a restaurant.
670.q: Yes. When I was with Buddy Johnson’s band. They had a rope down the middle of the dance hall and the black was on one side and white was on one side. But they all seemed to be enjoying themselves. And I went in a liquor store one time down there and they had a rope down the middle of the liquor…

214.t: Segregation on the road with a mixed band
214.s: A mixed band met segregated hotels, refused service and aggressive state troopers.
214.q: Well we didn’t have any trouble, we just had to, we couldn’t stay at the same hotels. I remember Richmond, Virginia, Jackie Byard and Rufus Jones were on the band, and we had to take them to a colored hotel, and then we came back to ours. And of course they could eat there at their own hotel, but…

1012.t: What made his father angry: unprepared players and racism
1012.s: Unprepared musicians on Sound Pieces, segregation in St. Louis, Black, Brown and Beautiful, and Self Help is Needed.
1012.q: Probably lack of preparation for musicians that he had to work with. He would get really pretty upset about that. It’s funny you mentioned “Sound Pieces.” Well you know the piece itself was pretty difficult with the bass clar — [scats]. Well they couldn’t play it. When they first were recording…

661.t: Mother with the International Sweethearts of Rhythm on the road
661.s: Her mother described segregation, danger and strict rules while touring the South with the all-female band.
661.q: Well when she was with the International Sweethearts of Rhythm in the 40s, which was, there were several, probably many all-female bands and orchestras back then during World War II when all the men went overseas. But this orchestra started from a school,

906.t: Jim Crow on the road: she noticed nothing
906.s: Fillius asks about segregation on tour; Jillean says she never noticed any and had misunderstood the question at first.
906.ch: Meeting Joe and life with the Basie band
906.q: I didn’t notice it. I didn’t think about it. And I would not go to a place where obviously it would not be approved that Joe and I were together.

477.t: First encounter with segregation joining the Dorsey band in Shreveport
477.s: At twenty he flew to Shreveport to join the Jimmy Dorsey band and met segregated water, bathrooms and restaurants for the first time; he describes Lee Castaldo leading the band.
477.ch: The Dorsey band and the road
477.q: I mean yes, but only in those days no. I was really colorblind. But then when I first went with the Dorsey band, which was — this was a hell of a lot later — this would be when I was 20 I went with the Dorsey band and I was going to meet them in Shreveport, Louisiana. And I took the milk plane…

984.t: On the road with Nellie Lutcher and segregated lodging
984.s: On the 1958 Lutcher tour the sidemen stayed in black hotels and kitchens while she stayed downtown; he discusses his reaction.
984.ch: Nellie Lutcher and Lambert, Hendricks & Ross
984.q: I went out with Nellie in January of ’58 for four months and then let’s see, I guess Christmas of ’58, the Christmas holidays, three weeks, I went to Chicago for three weeks with Phineas Newborn.

61.s: Refused service in a Los Angeles restaurant, Mahalia dined in her room; a Houston policeman stop and her laugh.
61.q: hired him at Columbia, and it continued. It may or may not have contributed to his death. I never asked. I said, “Let’s take Mahalia out to dinner,” because I would look up Mahalia if I was ever in a town where she was. We went to this very fine restaurant that Irving knew about. It was a little on…

85.t: Integrated band with Buddy Rich, Art Pepper and Joe Albany
85.s: Carter says he had no difficulty with white players, tells of the St. Louis dancers asking about his pianist, and discusses Art Pepper's book.
85.q: Actually, I never encountered any difficulty with that. I might just tell you one little anecdote about when we played at a club called the Plantation. I think it was in St. Louis, and Joe Albany was playing on the piano, you know, chair. Actually, he was playing on the piano, from the piano chair.…

503.t: Golf lessons and segregated courses with Ray Brown
503.s: He took a lesson from Charlie Sifford but he and Brown were refused entry to a Virginia course.
503.ch: Oscar Peterson and moving to New York
503.q: him on a golf course somewhere and Ray said, “Would you please give us a lesson?” And Charlie said, “Sure.” So we spent about an hour with him and so that was, one of the feathers in my cap is taking a lesson with the great Charlie Sifford. But on the other hand I remember Ray Brown and I going on…

558.s: In the South Kenton used his Cuban passport to smooth hotel problems; Camero says he keeps to music and was the only black member.
558.q: Well that was mostly over there in the south mostly, yes. But then, as I had at that time, I had a passport. I still had a Cuban passport at that time so then things were made smoother.

105.t: A mixed group in a segregated America
105.s: Hamilton says his sense of humor differs from other black people, recalls the Pittsburgh Carrier headline calling his group all white, and tells of hotel and gas-station discrimination.
105.ch: Race, family and the younger generation
105.q: You know, in all honesty I think the most important thing is the fact that what I realize -- the difference between me and other black people, let’s put it like that right, is my sense of humor was entirely different because what I thought was funny wasn’t funny to them at all.

470.t: The orchestra's Carnegie Hall trip, living with athletes and mixed bands
470.s: A restaurant refusal on the orchestra trip, Ernst Hoffman's response, roommate Milt Campbell and the racially mixed fraternity jobs and jam sessions.
470.ch: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
470.q: Baltimore Colts. So we had some isolated instances of integration. I can remember the first tour we took with the orchestra. I was in the orchestra, and we went to play at Carnegie Hall. But we had to pay our way by bus clear there. I can remember them calling ahead, for all the stops that we were…

86.t: White musicians and fans in the South; enduring for his mother's sake
86.s: College musicians sat in with the band, and Edison explains why they kept their composure.
86.q: A lot of musicians used to come around, especially from those colleges, a lot of guys down there that were studying music like Southern University, University of Texas, the University of Georgia, Georgia Tech… played in Florida and they had some white musicians down there that would come and sit on…

107.t: Segregated audiences on the 1953 Southern tour
107.s: The band played roped-off dances and halls where blacks sat in balconies, and some members resented Basie accepting such dates.
107.ch: Joining Basie and life on the road
107.q: Yeah, or maybe it was the other way around. Sugar Ray was the butt of all the jokes, and Scotty was the funny man. We had some vocal quartets like -- I call them “bird groups.” Not the Orioles. Not someone that big in stature, but -- oh, we had Billy Ward and the Dominoes, and a lesser-known other…

371.t: Segregation, the 1947 Jackson lunch counter, and Norman Granz
371.s: Jones recalls discrimination at a Jackson, Michigan lunch counter in 1947 and praises Norman Granz's insistence on integrated audiences; a drive through Vicksburg with Hot Lips Page.
371.ch: Pontiac childhood, family and piano training
371.q: Pontiac is a good place to be from… I don't know anything about Vicksburg. It was a southern town. If I had grown up there, I would've been subject all the segregation and all of the discrimination that was rife at the time, and lasted well into the 1940s. As a matter of fact, when I was with JTP,…

224.t: Bus travel with Luis Russell and seeing racism in the South
224.s: Tired of the bus, he saw outright racial attitudes in Maryland and followed his father's way of working around them.
224.ch: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
224.q: After – I stayed with the band a year, like I said. We would travel by bus. I was tired of that bus after the first year. And growing up in Boston, we’d get to places like Maryland. To see the attitude with some people with that race situation. That was my first time seeing it outright. It was…

451.t: Racism on the road and alcohol
451.s: Segregation affected touring in mixed groups, with Sonny Rollins and others; alcohol was a danger for him.
451.ch: Touring, Ella Fitzgerald and South America
451.q: Sorry. Well, I mentioned… this is a fact (unintelligible). As you know, the, the black-white racial thing, even Jewish, uh, Baptists… (laughs) Humans aren’t perfect. I assume we’ll never be, but the racial thing was pretty tacky in those days, and I

108.t: Sam Donahue's band and segregation in Harrisburg and Washington
108.s: Refused pool and pepperburgers, he and white bandmates meet discrimination; the band is otherwise warm.
108.q: was a small group: one trumpet, he playing alto, Frank playing trombone, and a rhythm section. We also had a guitar player. Rudy Cafaro was a guitar player. It was a nice little group. We played things like Dardanelle, that Herbie was famous for. But Sam Donahue’s band, I loved that band, because…

114.t: Eight years with the quintet; the South after integration
114.s: He traveled the world for eight years; going back South after integration he was fawned over, but he just wanted to be left alone.
114.q: 8 years. 8 years. Yeah. Yeah. Everywhere, man. Japan, Africa, you know. [indiscernible] I mean, everywhere. Australia. You know what? I went all over the world. The only place I didn't go, India. Everywhere I go now, like I was just in Athens, oh, man. I was in Istanbul. I was in Stockholm. And…

464.t: Virginia Beach: Slide Hampton's band and the segregated beach
464.s: While working a Virginia Beach club in about 1963, a suntan lotion incident shows the segregation and ends the band's engagement early.
464.q: I met Dizzy in 1959, the first time. Then, when I was working with Slide Hampton in ’62 or ’63, we worked in Virginia Beach. I keep saying, I’m going to have to

64.t: San Antonio with Slam Stewart and the segregated waiting room
64.s: Slam's group flopped in San Antonio against Amos Milburn's blues, and on the way home they were bumped from a plane and kept moving around a colored sign.
64.ch: Sideman years and the European tour
64.q: said, “He is really something”. I tried to explain and I was at a loss for words as to how to tell her, she’s not a musician… but to tell her how different he was. But as I remember, the thing that impressed me was the way he played changes. He played changes like nobody I’d ever… he and Kenny…

109.t: Jacksonville drugstore: trombonist George Washington looks out for him
109.s: On the way south George Washington went with him into a Jacksonville drugstore to show him how to behave, as Clarke bought toiletries.
109.ch: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
109.q: Now, when we went to Jacksonville -- now this is strange. Now, George Washington, the trombone player, well, they all knew that I had never been south. So we kind of stopped -- we were in Jacksonville, so we kind of stopped --

137.t: Politicians, racketeers and segregation trouble at the pier
137.s: Wires were cut on the pier, and his plan for a night for whites drew complaints of segregating from black musicians.
137.ch: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
137.q: Yeah, well, it hurt them so bad until they started to -- I was playing out on the pier, too. Came there one night and all the wires was cut. So I went to the D.A. and he made them give me some light on Sunday. And hook up to anything.

230.t: Touring the South with a mixed band
230.s: Barnet says his mixed band had little trouble, mostly playing college dates and insisting on the mixed band in advance, while Willard recounts other bands' problems.
230.q: They were afraid of the deep south at the time. They said they'd lose every -- and I never had that problem. I was down there with a mixed band and I didn't -- outside of the fact that the guys' accomodations at times were pretty raunchy, we never had any trouble on the job, anybody that took…

65.s: They were well treated, invited to see Walter Winchell, because Cubans were not considered black.
65.ch: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
65.q: Yeah, the Beachcomber, and we was there about ten or eleven out of my band, and we were received and we enjoyed tremendously.

87.t: Boyd Raeburn's tours and who enforced segregation
87.s: Raeburn's band toured New England, Jersey and Virginia; often the proprietor, not the law, objected to a mixed band.
87.q: Well, we toured New England, and we toured Jersey. We didn't go too far. We'd play around West Virginia and Washington, D. C. It used to be a kind of problem around there, you know. And near parts of Virginia around Washington.

88.t: The Ted Heath package tour and warnings about Birmingham
88.s: The package with Ted Heath, June Christie and Gary Morton was warned that Birmingham did not want white and black acts on one stage.
88.q: Yeah, because there were headlines in the paper. So, well, they didn't want acts mixed, you know, they didn't want white and black acts on the same stage in Birmingham, Alabama. But we were warned before we went there that they didn't want it and that there might be trouble. And so we went ahead…

166.t: Segregated dance in Atlanta and the 'colored nanny' remark
166.s: A chicken-wire divided dance in Atlanta, and Simmons's retort to a white man.
166.ch: With Benny Goodman and Louis Armstrong
166.q: Boy, but that Louis Armstrong tour was something else, baby. We got to Atlanta, Georgia and they had chicken wire down through the middle of this auditorium. It was a dance. Whites on one side, blacks on the other. If the dance gets too good, the blacks got to leave, you know. If the music got too…

89.t: Southern Rhodesia and the Sports Car Club of America
89.s: On a State Department tour of Africa the band had no problems in Salisbury, and Benny Morton and he were welcomed at a race meet because of his Sports Car Club blazer.
89.q: : Well, being an auto bug brings to my mind our engagement in Southern Rhodesia, Salisbury, to be exact. You know, that's the country where they have the double standard, you know, one standard for Africans and one standard for the non-Africans. There are signs on all the buildings saying that we…

28.t: Amy sings 'Ole Man River' on the ship home
28.s: On the ship back, the singer Amy was pressed to sing Ole Man River; when she sang the original lyric's slur everyone fled, leaving Bill Coleman's foster daughter bewildered.
28.ch: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
28.q: and got all our ladyfriend, and there were some English people who followed us all around and there was a certain girl, tall beautiful girl, but she was just tall and beautiful. Her name was Amy. Well, Amy could sing, she had a deep voice, you know, a contralto voice, but it was a pleasant voice,…

381.t: Chitlin-circuit one-nighters and a racial insult in Goldsboro
381.s: Three months without a night off on the black circuit, and a hostess announcing 'a hot nigger band' in Goldsboro, North Carolina.
381.q: And we used to have, like a string of one nighters, three straight months without a night off -- I mean we played all of the chitlin circuits, we used to call them, because it was all black dancers, all except maybe one or two white dancers who were thrown in on a Saturday night.

120.t: Segregation in Fort Lauderdale and Lake Tahoe with an integrated band
120.s: At Fascio's Supper Club his Black sidemen face bomb threats and cannot find rooms, and at Lake Tahoe no one will house them.
120.ch: Looking back and the lean years
120.q: took me over to the side and he said - I didn't know you had any colored guys in the band -- I said, well, what's the difference? He said, well, Jesus, the colored people don't work together with white down here and I said - well, Christ, this is a hell of a time to tell me. I said, the booking…

453.t: Segregation ends the Pass in Review tour and Armstrong calls
453.s: Because Black and white performers could not share a stage in the South, the show dumped them; then Armstrong, courted by both Mezzrow and Glaser as manager, contacted Randolph.
453.ch: Sunset Cafe, Pass in Review and rebuilding the band
453.q: Well, at this time, this was 'way before Martin Luther King had had his walk.

383.t: Segregated hotels on tour and the Goodman films
383.s: Wilson and Hampton stayed in Negro hotels rather than fight each town, and the band films first excluded and then carefully separated the quartet.
383.ch: Later career and The Benny Goodman Story
383.q: Yes, but that was -- it's hard to call that a problem because it was the norm of that day. We didn't challenge the norm, which was that Lionel and I couldn't stay in the white hotels. If we'd had to make a battle of that thing in every town on one-night stands; you couldn't ever get to work, making…

92.t: Henderson's band in Mississippi: the Rosedale sandwich shop
92.s: On the road in Mississippi, a white man in Rosedale told Collins to stand outside because the place was too small for white folks and 'niggers.'
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: Oh, boy, oh, boy. Well, I'll give you an idea. I was in a little town, Rosedale we stopped, and I went into a little place to get a sandwich, so there was an old white man in there, and there was just the two of us. Nobody -- as a matter of fact no one was in there but him, and I went in and I…

388.t: Segregation on the road with Billie Holiday
388.s: Shaw's band refuses hotels that exclude anyone; on the southern tour Billie is made to eat in kitchens, so Leeman and others join her there, and a girls' college would not let her sing.
388.q: she sang on the bandstand and she roomed with Billie, and our past discussions about the racial question, one night in New England of all places, they didn't want to let us in the hotel because we were playing a college town, so Artie Shaw did not check in a hotel unless the whole band checked in,…

115.t: Woody Herman's Texas tour and Jake Hanna
115.s: Woody hired Jake Hanna to avoid Jim Crow in Texas, then phoned in surprise at integrated hotels.
115.q: Just like Woody Herman. Well, I played on the big bands, too, see. And I'm trying to -- let's see, I think it was -- about '65, when he went down -- no, 60-something, when Jake Hannah joined the band.

413.t: Rooming with Cootie Williams in segregated hotels
413.s: On Goodman's tours Maxwell registers for both of them in Ohio hotels; Cootie declines to make trouble.
413.q: Like when we were with Benny Goodman, joined the band. Well, I generally liked to room alone but we would get into a place like Ohio or someplace

79.t: French Canadian children touch the Black musicians
79.s: Traveling Michigan in a curtained bus, the band arrived at a Mackinaw ferry where children saw Black people for the first time and touched their hands to see if it rubbed off.
79.ch: Leaving St. Louis: Toby show, Darrell Harris and Eli Rice
79.q: No, I think he's out of, anyhow, I met him in Indiana. A nice little 10 piece band; so we were to open this in Michigan, work from Sault St. Marie and on down and on up, Mackinac Islands and all that sort of thing. And that was one place I'll never forget as long as I live. We got to a place…
